article.title: Jim Crow Said This Could Never Happen
article.author: Berry Craig
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Goldie Taylor, 80, and I grew up in small-town Mayfield, Kentucky, when Jim Crow segregation and race discrimination were both the law and the social order. I’m 76. Symbolic of the separate and unequal order, mayors were white men. “I never believed it would change,” said Taylor, who is my longtime friend and president of our Mayfield-Graves County NAACP branch. “I never dreamed we could ever have a Black mayor in the city of Mayfield.” Neither did I. But on November 3, voters in Mayfield, the seat of Graves County in westernmost Kentucky, elected Derrick Parrott, 41, to be the next mayor. My old hometown is nearly nearly 69 percent white. The outgoing mayor and her predecessor are white women. Though Parrott, the public-school system’s school/home/community liaison, has made history in Mayfield, population about 10,000, he doesn’t consider himself a history-maker. Related: Charles Booker Wants to Replace Mitch McConnell—and Shock Kentucky “I’m just ready to get to work,” said Parrott, who is wrapping up his fourth term on the city council. “I’m thinking about my city council team, my department heads, and making plans.” When Taylor and I were kids, white supremacy had been entrenched for decades in the former Confederate states and in border states like Kentucky. Our home state “had segregated racing, transportation, parks, hotels, theaters, library systems, orphans’ homes, restaurants, funeral parlors, and more,” wrote James C. Klotter and Craig Thompson Friend in A New history of Kentucky, Second Edition. Taylor and I remember the “more.” In Mayfield, “more” included segregated toilets at the Graves County courthouse marked “white” and “colored,” and the “colored” ward in the basement of Mayfield Hospital where I was born. Taylor lives on Tice Road in the same neighborhood where he grew up. More than a few Mayfield whites called it “N----rtown,” a common racist epithet for Black communities everywhere in America. Taylor and I remember the Princess Theater from our youth. Had we known each other as friends then, we couldn’t have taken in a movie together. The Princess was white only downstairs. Blacks had to sit in the balcony unless a movie drew a big crowd. Related: Hegseth’s Holy War on Fat Generals Meets the Weight of History If all the downstairs seats were filled, ushers would direct whites to the balcony, Taylor recalled. Nonetheless, ushers ensured that segregation prevailed. “There would be at least one empty row, maybe two, between the whites and the Blacks.” The ushers would force Blacks to the back of the balcony. If whites kept coming, Blacks “were told to go downstairs, get our money back, and go home. That happened to me and my brothers on a couple of occasions. We weren’t happy with it, but we knew there was nothing we could do about it.” My skin color permitted me to eat a meal or order ice cream or a soft drink in the dining area of any cafe, restaurant, diner, drug store soda fountain, or dime store lunch counter in Mayfield. Citizens with Taylor’s skin color had no such freedom. Taylor’s stepfather cooked at a little cafe. “If we wanted a hamburger from there, we had to go around to the back door. We’d step inside and order what we wanted. Right inside was a little table with two chairs. If we wanted to eat, we had to sit in the chairs.” Otherwise, Blacks had to eat outside or take food home. Taylor went to Dunbar School, a combination elementary, junior high, and high school. I started out at white-only Longfellow Elementary. At Dunbar, Taylor said, school supplies were mostly hand-me-downs from the white schools – “torn up, ragged, pages missing, backs off, written in. By the time we’d get the books, they were already outdated.” The Longfellow campus adjoined my backyard in a white working-class neighborhood. When I was a kid, the only Blacks I saw on my street were a woman who was a maid and a man who came weekly to collect trash in a mule-drawn wooden wagon that rolled on car wheels and tires. Related: JD Vance, Abdul El-Sayed and the GOP’s Search for a Racist Sweet Spot One day when I was around 12, he came with his son, who seemed to be about my age. While his dad went to get our burn barrel for emptying in the wagon bed, he and I visited. It was the first time I had had any interaction with a Black kid. Yet I didn’t think about why no Black families lived where we lived. It was a casual conversation with another Black kid that jarred me into recognizing the reality of Jim Crow, not only the inherent injustice of the system, but also the hypocrisy of those who perpetrated or acquiesced in it. Like many youngsters getting acquainted, we asked each other where our fathers worked. “General Tire,” I said. “My father’s a Presbyterian minister,” he said. I was floored. “Where?” I asked incredulously. “Right here in Mayfield,” he answered. I went to First Presbyterian with my parents and my brother. The pastors and the congregants were white. The only Blacks I ever saw in the church were a nursery worker and the janitor. I had been taught in Sunday school that we are all God’s children and that God loves us all the same. But Black Presbyterians were not welcome in the church of my youth. Segregation was crumbling by the time I graduated from Mayfield High School in 1967 and went off to nearby Murray State University to study history. My experience was not unlike that of Charles B. Dew, one of my favorite Civil War historians. He went off to Williams College in Massachusetts from Jim Crow Florida. History taught him to recognize what he called “collective white blindness.” I learned that Jim Crow was America’s apartheid which grotesquely mocked The Pledge of Allegiance, especially its last six words: with liberty and justice for all . “The embrace of Jim Crow as a way of life and a system of beliefs for white southerners was powerful and seductive,” Dew wrote in The Making of a Racist . “White supremacy is a noxious weed that plants deep roots. I know this first-hand. But I also know that racism can be overcome.” In an interview with Robin Lindley posted on BillMoyers.com, Dew, at age 89, an emeritus professor of history at his undergrad alma mater (He has a PhD in history from Johns Hopkins), said that when he taught Southern history, he used “his own stories to illustrate points about the South and the culture.” I did likewise when I taught Kentucky and American history courses at West Kentucky Community and Technical College in Paducah. I shared with my students my first-hand stories about Jim Crow Mayfield, including the story about my chance conversation with the minister’s son. Parrott, a Mayfield High School and Murray State grad, represents “much needed change,” Taylor said. I heartily agree, and my wife and I would have happily voted for him had we not moved to nearby Arlington, her Carlisle County hometown, going on six years ago. In the 1960s, Congress, at President Lyndon B. Johnson’s urging, passed sweeping federal civil rights laws hailed as a “Second Reconstruction.” The landmark legislation was aimed at relegating Jim Crow to the trash heap of history where it so richly belonged. But bigotry persists. Donald Trump and his MAGA movement is Exhibit A. When Trump said he wanted to “Make America Great Again,” he meant an America ruled by white, straight, conservative Christian males, an America where women stayed home and raised the kids, where Blacks were invisible, where immigrants of color stayed away, and LGBTQ+ Americans stayed in the closet. Voters, at least for now, rebuked Trump and Trumpism at the polls on Nov. 3. “A broad coalition of Americans, including Republicans , independents, and those who had never voted before, decided to elect the most diverse, anti-establishment Congress in history,” wrote Ankita Rao in The Guardian . Voters also repudiated “some of the racist, xenophobic, transphobic, and other rhetoric that has escalated in recent years. Bo French, the Texas politician who had posted a racist diatribe about south Asian students at a football game, lost his election , along with Vivek Ramaswamy and his abhorrent attack ad , Ken Paxton with his transphobic AI ads, and Mike Collins and his multiple associations with neo-Nazis. At a time when the Trump administration itself peddles racist tropes on its X account and at rallies, there were tears of relief and cautious hope of an era of decency.” Goldie Taylor and I share that hope.
